newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-zone stability council gains grudging acceptance.
newsitem.headline: Euro-zone stability council gains grudging acceptance.

text.p: France's call for a special council to co-ordinate economic policy inside monetary union appears to have won grudging acceptance, though it has been stripped of most of its powers even before its inception.

Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told a news conference after a meeting of EU finance minsters on Monday that it would be hard to prevent ministers inside the euro-zone meeting informally if they wanted to.
"There is a consensus to say that something of this kind will be set up. There is no consensus on the need to set it up," Zalm, whose country holds the European Union presidency, said.

Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink noted France and Germany wanted the council, though Sweden was sceptical about any reduction in the power of the ECOFIN, the council which groups all 15 finance ministers.
"Of course nothing prevents ministers from different countries meeting. One cannot prohibit this," he told reporters.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel confirmed last week that they agreed there should be an informal "stability council", which would discuss economic policies among countries inside the euro-zone.
But the agreement between Europe's two biggest economies appears to have irritated some of the EU's smaller countries.
Diplomats said there were fears about setting up such a body outside established EU rules and treaties, which provide protection for smaller countries and ensure a role for the European Commission.
The idea also prompted criticism earlier this year from some members of the Bundesbank, who feared it might be used to undermine the independence of the future European Central Bank.
Other officials have complained such a council could cut Europe in two, between those inside monetary union and those waiting to joining or choosing not to do so.
"We want to avoid having a division into two teams, into an 'A-team' and a 'B-team'," Asbrink said. He added that though the issue was discussed on Monday, no formal decision was made.
The council, first proposed by France as a counterweight to the European Central Bank, now appears to have worn down resistance on the grounds it will have very little power.

"The stability council is an informal club bringing together countries in the euro zone. It should not be a counterweight to the European Central Bank. It should be a complement to the European Central Bank," Zalm said.
"This club should not have any power to take decisions," Zalm, speaking through an interpreter, added.
He said it would have no competence to set currency policy, which would remain in the hands of finance ministers from all member states and the European Central Bank.
In what appeared to be a requirement towards winning German acceptance, Arthuis pledged last week that the council would not issue proposals on currencies.

France has said the council would oversee budgetary policies among countries in the euro-zone, ensuring they stuck to a pledge to limit budget deficits after the launch of monetary union on January 1, 1999.
Arthuis repeated on Monday that the council would be informal, like the Group of Seven rich nations forum, which has no structure nor permanent secretariat.
But ministers have left vague exactly what it will do, and when it will meet. France has suggested it meet both at the level of finance ministers and heads of state, like the G7.
"If ministers meet informally they can discuss anything that comes into their heads, including the weather forecast for the next day," Zalm said.
